content: Cotton swabs, also known as cotton buds in British English, are versatile tools commonly used in first aid, cosmetic applications, and various other purposes. They are composed of a small wad of cotton wrapped around the end of a slender rod, which can be made of wood, rolled paper, or plastic. The most typical use involves dipping the cotton tip into a substance and then using the swab as an applicator for that substance. In some cases, swabs are employed to remove substances, such as earwax from the ear canal. However, the accompanying instructions often include a warning against inserting the swab directly into the ear, as this practice is hazardous. Using a swab in this manner can puncture the eardrum and only remove a small portion of the wax, which is visible on the swab. The majority of the wax is pushed deeper into the ear canal, potentially causing further complications. The invention of the cotton swab is attributed to Leo Gerstenzang in 1923. His product, initially named Baby Gays, eventually became the widely recognized brand Q-tip. Traditional cotton swabs typically feature a single tip on a wooden handle and are still frequently used, particularly in medical settings. These swabs are usually about six inches (15 cm) long and are often packaged sterile, either singly or in pairs, within paper or plastic sleeves. The paper sleeve and wooden handle allow the package to be autoclaved for sterilization, as plastic sleeves or handles would melt in the autoclave. Medical-grade swabs are often utilized for microbiological cultures. They are swabbed onto or into the infected area and then wiped across a culture medium, such as an agar plate, where any bacteria from the swab can grow. These swabs are also used to collect DNA samples, most commonly from the inner cheek. Additionally, they can be employed to apply medications to specific areas, selectively remove substances from targeted regions, or apply cleaning agents like Betadine. Cotton swabs are also available in shorter lengths, typically around 6 cm, and are often double-tipped. The handles were initially made of wood, later replaced by rolled paper, which remains the most common material, although tubular plastic handles are gaining popularity. These swabs are frequently sold in large quantities, sometimes 300 or more per container. A recent innovation involves a specialized type of double-tipped cotton swab designed for over-the-counter drug application. These swabs feature hollow tubular plastic handles filled with medication. Breaking one marked end of the swab releases an air seal, allowing the medication to saturate the cotton at the opposite end for direct application. Cotton swabs are available in a variety of colors, such as purple, fuchsia, pink, and green, although the cotton itself remains white.
